ingredients.name: Dried sprats (halmasso)
ingredients.notes: heads removed; soaked in water for 10-15 minutes then drained and dried on paper towels -- this removes excess salt and softens the fish

ingredients.name: Tomato
ingredients.notes: sliced; adds moisture and slight sourness

ingredients.name: Lime
ingredients.notes: juiced; added at the very end

ingredients.name: Salt
ingredients.notes: taste before adding any -- dried sprats are already very salty from the curing process

steps.instruction: Remove the heads from the dried sprats if not already done. Soak in cold water for 10-15 minutes to reduce excess saltiness and soften slightly. Drain thoroughly and pat dry with paper towels -- excess moisture will cause the sprats to steam rather than fry crisply.

Heat the coconut oil in a flat pan or wok over medium heat. Add the sprats in a single layer and fry for 2-3 minutes, gently turning once, until lightly golden and crispy. Remove and set aside. Do not over-fry -- they should be crisp but not dried out.
In the same pan, add the mustard seeds and let them splutter. Add the cinnamon, cardamom, curry leaves, and pandan leaf and sauté for 30 seconds.
Add the onion, garlic, ginger (if using), and green chillies. Stir-fry over medium-high heat for 3-4 minutes until the onion is golden and slightly caramelised.
Add the chilli powder, turmeric, and black pepper. Stir for 30 seconds to toast the spices.
Add the tomato and a splash of water (about 2-3 tablespoons). Mix well, cover, and cook for 2-3 minutes until the tomato softens into the spice base.
Add the fried sprats back into the pan. Toss gently to coat in the spice-onion base. Cook uncovered for 1-2 more minutes, tossing carefully to avoid breaking the small fish.

Squeeze in the lime juice just before serving. Taste -- if the sprats are already very salty from the curing process, no extra salt is needed. Serve hot with red rice and pol sambol for a classic Sri Lankan village breakfast or lunch.

source_site: islandsmile.org, cross-checked against flavorsofadiva.com, dailylife.lk, tiktok @nipcooks, srilankan.cooking, mylankanfoodjournal.com, topsrilankanrecipe.com, pachakam.com, and dailyfoodrecipes.com
collection_method: scraped, cross-checked across 9+ independent sources; very strong agreement on the soak-then-fry-separately technique and the critical importance of not over-salting
notes: Halmasso theldala (tempered dried sprats) is described across multiple sources as the quintessential Sri Lankan village breakfast -- red rice, dhal curry, pol sambol, and tempered sprats on a banana leaf is considered a deeply comforting and emotionally resonant meal. The pre-soak (like karawala curry sl_038) is important for both reducing excess saltiness and removing any sand or grit from the drying process; salt should always be tasted and added minimally or not at all. Two versions exist: a dry tempered version (this entry) and a wet curry version with coconut milk (halmasso curry) -- sources agree the dry stir-fry is more commonly eaten for everyday meals, while the coconut-milk curry version is richer and slightly less common. Dried sprats can also be replaced by dried anchovies in most international markets.
